profiles.name: Christopher Saur II
profiles.description: Christopher Saur II was a Germantown printer and German Baptist Brethren pacifist. Authorities imprisoned him in May 1778 over opposition to warfare and refusal of an allegiance oath. An Andrews University study records release on May 29; accounts disagree on the arrest day. His property was later confiscated. He was a Brethren member, distinct from his father and his son of the same name.

profiles.name: Herman Husband
profiles.description: Herman Husband was a Quaker farmer and pamphleteer who became the leading voice of the North Carolina Regulators. For his agitation against colonial corruption he was jailed and, in 1770, expelled from the colonial Assembly and outlawed; he fled the colony before the Battle of Alamance. A generation later, having settled in western Pennsylvania, he was swept up in the Whiskey Rebellion of 1794 — arrested as a suspected leader and imprisoned for months in Philadelphia. Released in failing health, he died on the journey home in 1795.
profiles.finding: Completed identity-specific historical search; text, contextual imagery or insufficiently linked namesakes did not establish usable portrait.

profiles.name: Israel Pemberton
profiles.description: Israel Pemberton was a Philadelphia Quaker also known as Israel Pemberton Jr. He was a wealthy Philadelphia merchant and philanthropist so influential among Friends that critics called him "the King of the Quakers." He was one of the "Virginia Exiles" — about twenty prominent Philadelphia Quakers whom the Continental Congress and the Pennsylvania Supreme Executive Council arrested in September 1777, as the British approached the city, and banished without any charge or trial to the frontier town of Winchester, Virginia, for the Society of Friends' conscientious refusal to support the Revolutionary War. Held roughly seven months, the survivors were released in the spring of 1778. His health was broken by the ordeal, and he died within a year of his release.
profiles.finding: PAFA portrait is son Joseph Pemberton; APS diary illustration is James Pemberton; neither substitutes for Israel.

profiles.name: Philip Wigle
profiles.description:
Philip Wigle was a western Pennsylvania farmer-distiller and Whiskey Rebellion (1791-94) participant who beat federal tax collector Robert Johnson and burned his home in protest of Alexander Hamilton's excise tax on whiskey. One of only two men convicted of treason (the rebellion produced the first treason convictions in the new United States). Sentenced to hang; pardoned by President George Washington on November 2, 1795.

Philip Vigol (also spelled Wigle or Weigel) was a western Pennsylvania farmer who took part in the Whiskey Rebellion of 1794, the uprising against Alexander Hamilton’s federal excise tax on whiskey; he had assaulted a tax collector and burned his house. In 1795 he and John Mitchell became the first two people ever convicted of treason against the United States, under a sweeping definition of treason as “levying war” by resisting a federal law. Both were sentenced to hang, but President George Washington pardoned them.

profiles.name: Samuel Rowland Fisher
profiles.description: Samuel Rowland Fisher was a Philadelphia Quaker merchant. He was one of the "Virginia Exiles" — about twenty prominent Philadelphia Quakers whom the Continental Congress and the Pennsylvania Supreme Executive Council arrested in September 1777, as the British approached the city, and banished without any charge or trial to the frontier town of Winchester, Virginia, for the Society of Friends' conscientious refusal to support the Revolutionary War. Held roughly seven months, the survivors were released in the spring of 1778. Fisher continued to refuse allegiance to the new government; in 1779 he was arrested and charged as a Tory over a letter to his brother in New York, and — refusing to recognize the court's authority — was imprisoned in Philadelphia for about two years, keeping a journal of his confinement.
